summary: ModVault is a minimal 4626-style share vault: deposits mint shares priced off asset.balanceOf(vault) plus whatever the wired strategy reports in totalAssets(), withdrawals burn shares and pull any shortfall from the strategy, and the owner may point the vault at any strategy and push idle capital into it. Control flow is checks-effects-interactions and no reentrancy path was found, but the pricing model is unprotected on three sides: a first depositor can inflate the share price with a donation and steal from or block later deposits (VAULT-1); the owner can move 100% of deposits into an arbitrary strategy in one transaction with no timelock and no way to recall funds (VAULT-2, VAULT-5); and the vault pays withdrawals off the strategy's self-reported total, which for the catalog's fixed-yield strategy includes unbacked phantom accrual, so early withdrawers are paid from other depositors' principal (VAULT-3). The performance fee never collects because harvest() compares totalAssets to itself (VAULT-4). It is not safe to deploy as-is for third-party funds; it is acceptable as a single-operator or test vault when the governor port is a timelock, the first deposit is seeded by the deployer, and the strategy reserve is funded ahead of accrual.

findings.title: First-depositor share inflation: a 1-wei deposit plus a direct donation lets an attacker steal from or brick later deposits
findings.where: convertToShares() L44-L49, totalAssets() L38-L42, deposit() L57-L64
findings.detail: Shares are priced off asset.balanceOf(vault) with no virtual offset, no dead shares and no minimum deposit. convertToShares returns `assets` 1:1 when totalSupply==0, so the first depositor can own the entire supply with 1 share, then transfer assets straight to the vault to push the price per share arbitrarily high. Every later deposit is floored to a handful of shares (or to 0, which reverts ZERO_SHARES), and the rounding remainder accrues to the attacker's share. The vault is deployed by a composer with no seeding step, so every fresh deployment sits in this state until someone deposits.
findings.exploit: 1) Fresh vault, supply 0. Attacker deposit(1, attacker) -> 1 share. 2) Attacker asset.transfer(vault, 10_000e18) -> totalAssets = 10_000e18+1, supply 1. 3) Victim deposit(19_999e18, victim) -> shares = 19_999e18 * 1 / (10_000e18+1) = 1. Supply 2, totalAssets ~29_999e18. 4) Attacker withdraw(1, attacker) -> 14_999.5e18; ~4_999.5e18 of the victim's deposit is taken. Any victim depositing <= 10_000e18 instead reverts ZERO_SHARES, so the attacker can also block the vault outright at that price.
findings.recommendation: Adopt the OpenZeppelin 4626 virtual-shares/assets offset (add 10**decimalsOffset to supply and 1 to assets in both conversions), or mint a fixed dead-share amount to address(0) on the first deposit and require a minimum first deposit. Track assets with an internal accounting variable instead of balanceOf so donations cannot move the price.

findings.title: Owner can drain all deposits through setStrategy + allocate; no timelock, no honesty check on the strategy
findings.where: setStrategy() L82-L88, allocate() L95-L99, Owned.setOwner common.sol L47-L50
findings.detail: setStrategy accepts any contract whose asset() returns the right address; nothing verifies its deposit/withdraw behaviour or its totalAssets() report. allocate approves and pushes any amount of idle assets into it in one owner transaction. A strategy that simply keeps what it is sent, or that reports an inflated totalAssets(), gives the owner (or whoever obtains the owner key) 100% of user funds. Because totalAssets() is read live, the owner can also sandwich holders: setStrategy(0) makes the strategy's balance vanish from the price, owner deposits at the collapsed 1:1 price (L47 returns `assets` when total==0), then setStrategy(back) restores the assets and the owner's shares are now worth their pro-rata slice of everyone's capital. The catalog wires the owner port to an EOA by default ($owner) unless a governor block is connected.
findings.exploit: 1) Users deposit 1_000_000 USDC, all idle. 2) Owner deploys Sink with asset()==USDC, deposit(amount) doing transferFrom to itself, totalAssets() returning 0. 3) Owner setStrategy(Sink); allocate(1_000_000e6). 4) Sink holds the funds; vault totalAssets()==0; every user withdraw() computes assets=0 (or reverts on a zero push). Alternative sandwich: with 1_000_000 in the honest strategy and 1_000_000 shares outstanding, owner setStrategy(0) -> total 0; owner deposit(1_000_000e6) -> 1_000_000 shares at 1:1; owner setStrategy(strategy) -> total 2_000_000; owner withdraws 1_000_000 shares = 1_000_000 but the same trick works from any price above 1:1 and dilutes holders pro-rata to the accrued yield.
findings.recommendation: Wire the governor port to the timelock block for any deployment holding third-party funds and treat the vault as fully custodial otherwise. Make setStrategy withdraw everything from the old strategy first, revert if the new strategy's totalAssets() is nonzero on attach, and enforce a delay (announce/commit) before a new strategy can receive allocate(). Consider capping the fraction allocate can push per call.

findings.title: Share price trusts strategy.totalAssets() blindly; with the catalog strategy, phantom unbacked yield pays early withdrawers out of other depositors' principal
findings.where: totalAssets() L38-L42, withdraw() L66-L77; ModFixedYieldStrategy totalAssets()/_pending() strategy.sol L34-L42 and withdraw() L63-L70
findings.detail: convertToAssets prices every withdrawal off idle + strategy.totalAssets(), and withdraw() then asks the strategy for exactly that many assets without checking what came back or whether the strategy can pay it out of yield rather than principal. The only strategy in the catalog (ModFixedYieldStrategy) reports principal + accrued + _pending(), and _pending() is NOT capped by the reserve balance, so between interactions the reported figure drifts above what actually exists whenever the owner has not pre-funded the reserve (its default state: the reserve is funded by an optional fund() call). Its withdraw() pushes the requested amount from its whole balance, i.e. from other depositors' principal. Because accrual is linear in elapsed time and rateBps can be set as high as 100%/yr, a quiet vault drifts far above backing and the next withdrawer extracts the difference from everyone who stays. If the strategy's balance cannot cover the request, withdraw() reverts for everyone until the owner tops up.
findings.exploit: Strategy rate 10_000 bps, reserve 0. 1) Alice deposit(100) and Bob deposit(100); owner allocate(200); supply 200, principal 200. 2) Six months pass with no calls: strategy.totalAssets() = 200 + 0 + 100 phantom = 300. 3) Bob withdraw(100): assets = 100*300/200 = 150; idle 0 -> strategy.withdraw(150) -> _accrue realises 0 (backed=0) -> pushes 150 from principal. 4) Bob leaves with 150; strategy holds 50; Alice's 100 shares are now worth 50. At 12 months Bob's withdrawal would be 200 and Alice would be left with 0 (or the push reverts and Alice is locked until the owner funds).
findings.recommendation: Never pay out more than the strategy actually returns: measure balanceOf before/after strategy.withdraw and cap `assets` at the realised amount (or revert on shortfall). Prefer a strategy-side report that only counts backed yield (cap _pending by the reserve in totalAssets, not just in _accrue). Add a harvest/checkpoint that reconciles reported vs. actual assets, and document that the reserve must be funded ahead of accrual.

findings.title: harvest() can never collect a performance fee: `owed` is always exactly totalAssets(), so gain <= owed on every call
findings.detail: harvest computes gain = totalAssets() and owed = convertToAssets(totalSupply) = totalSupply * totalAssets() / totalSupply, which equals totalAssets() with no rounding. The early return at L106 therefore always fires, Harvested is never emitted and feeRecipient never receives shares. There is no stored high-water mark or last-harvest checkpoint against which a gain could be measured, so the performanceFeeBps parameter the deployer configures (default 10%) is dead. Users are not harmed as-is, but an operator relying on the fee for the yield reserve gets nothing, and the natural quick fix (compare against a stored total) without a high-water mark would let anyone re-charge fees on donations or on the same unrealised gain repeatedly, since harvest is permissionless.
findings.exploit: 1) Deploy with performanceFeeBps_=1000, fund the strategy reserve, deposit, allocate, wait a year so strategy reports +10%. 2) Anyone calls harvest(): gain = T, owed = T*S/S = T, `gain <= owed` -> returns 0. 3) feeRecipient balance stays 0 forever regardless of realised yield.
findings.recommendation: Store `lastTotalAssets` (a high-water mark) updated on deposit/withdraw/harvest; in harvest, fee = (totalAssets - lastTotalAssets) * bps / 10_000 when positive, mint shares for the fee using the post-fee price (shares = fee * supply / (total - fee)), then set the mark. Add a test that asserts harvest mints after accrual.

findings.title: No path to pull capital back from a strategy; changing strategies strands funds and collapses the share price
findings.where: setStrategy() L82-L88, allocate() L95-L99, withdraw() L71-L74
findings.detail: The only call the vault ever makes to strategy.withdraw is on the user-withdraw path, and only against the current strategy. setStrategy replaces the pointer without withdrawing from the previous strategy, so everything parked there instantly drops out of totalAssets(). ModFixedYieldStrategy.withdraw is gated to msg.sender == vault once setVault has run, so the vault is the only party able to recover those funds, and it will never call the old address again. There is no deallocate() or emergency withdraw for the owner either, so an honest operator rotating strategies, or pausing by setting address(0), locks depositors' capital and crashes the share price to idle/supply, which lets anyone buy shares at the crashed price and cash out once the pointer is restored.
findings.exploit: 1) 1_000 assets deposited, owner allocate(1_000) to StrategyA. 2) Owner deploys StrategyB and calls setStrategy(B) intending to migrate. 3) totalAssets() == 0; every withdraw() computes 0 assets (shares burned for nothing) and StrategyA's 1_000 is unreachable by anyone. 4) A watcher deposits 10 at total==0 -> gets 10 shares (L47) at 1:1; owner notices and calls setStrategy(A) back; watcher's shares are now priced against 1_010 total plus the legacy supply, taking value from original holders.
findings.recommendation: In setStrategy, if the current strategy is nonzero, call strategy.withdraw(strategy.totalAssets()) (or a full-exit function) before switching and revert on shortfall. Add an owner-only deallocate(amount) and an emergency path that returns to idle. Reject deposits while totalAssets()==0 and totalSupply>0 (see VAULT-6).

findings.title: Deposits made while totalSupply > 0 and totalAssets == 0 are minted 1:1 into legacy supply and are immediately diluted
findings.detail: The `supply == 0 || total == 0` branch returns `assets` shares. When supply is nonzero but total is zero (strategy reported a total loss, or a strategy pointer swap per VAULT-5), a new depositor's `assets` shares are added to the existing dead supply, so they own only assets/(supply+assets) of the vault. Once any value reappears (strategy recovers, pointer restored, donation), most of the newcomer's deposit belongs to the legacy holders. For an 18-decimal asset with a formerly large vault, a modest deposit can be almost entirely lost.
findings.exploit: 1) Vault had 1_000_000e18 deposited and allocated; strategy is hacked and reports totalAssets()==0; supply stays 1_000_000e18. 2) Newcomer deposit(1_000e18) -> shares = 1_000e18 (1:1). 3) Strategy is later made whole or the vault is re-pointed; total = 1_001_000e18 (or just the newcomer's 1_000e18 idle). 4) Newcomer's share of the vault is 1_000/1_001_000 ~ 0.1%: withdraw(1_000e18 shares) returns ~1e18 of the 1_000e18 deposited; legacy holders absorb the rest.
findings.recommendation: Revert deposits when totalSupply > 0 and totalAssets() == 0 (the vault is insolvent and must be reset by governance), or use the virtual-offset conversion from VAULT-1 so the price is never a degenerate 1:1 while shares exist.

findings.title: Fee-on-transfer assets mint shares for tokens never received; non-bool-returning tokens (USDT-style) cannot be used at all
findings.where: deposit() L59-L61, allocate() L97, SafeTransfer.pull/push common.sol L121-L127
findings.detail: deposit() prices shares from the nominal `assets` argument and only then pulls, so a token that burns or taxes on transfer credits the depositor with shares backed by more than the vault actually received; the shortfall is socialised onto existing holders and the last withdrawer takes a loss. Separately, SafeTransfer requires a bool return from transfer/transferFrom, and allocate() decodes a bool from approve, so tokens that return nothing (USDT, BNB on mainnet) revert on every deposit, withdraw and allocate, and USDT's approve also reverts when a nonzero allowance is overwritten (allocate leaves residual allowance if the strategy pulls less than approved). The catalog's own token block is a plain ERC20, so this only bites when the asset port is wired to an external token.
findings.exploit: Asset charges a 2% transfer tax. 1) Alice deposit(100) -> 100 shares; vault receives 98. 2) Bob deposit(100) -> shares = 100*100/98 = 102; vault receives 98 more (196 total). 3) Bob withdraw(102) -> assets = 102*196/202 = 98.97 (minus tax on the way out); Alice withdraw(100) gets the remaining ~97; each deposit round leaks the tax onto whoever exits last, and a depositor can repeatedly deposit/withdraw to grind the price down against passive holders.
findings.recommendation: Measure balanceOf before/after pull and mint shares on the delta. Use a safe-transfer helper that tolerates empty return data (OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 semantics) and safeApprove-to-zero before setting a new allowance. Document that rebasing and fee-on-transfer assets are unsupported.

findings.title: withdraw() burns shares even when they round to zero assets; deposit/withdraw accept address(0) receivers
findings.detail: withdraw requires shares > 0 but not assets > 0; when the share price is high (VAULT-1 donation, or a large-supply vault with a small share count) a small `shares` amount converts to 0 assets and the shares are burned for nothing. deposit(assets, address(0)) mints shares to the zero address (ERC20Base has no zero check), permanently locking the assets, and withdraw(shares, address(0)) will silently send assets to the zero address for tokens that allow it.
findings.exploit: 1) After the VAULT-1 donation the price is 10_000e18 per share. 2) A holder integrating via a UI that withdraws in share units calls withdraw(1, self) expecting dust: assets = 1*T/S computed normally, fine; but a holder with a fractional position that has been floored, e.g. shares=1 in a vault where T/S < 1 (after a strategy loss), gets assets = 0, the share is burned and the Withdraw event reports 0. 3) Any front-end that passes receiver=0 by mistake loses the deposit outright.
findings.recommendation: require(assets > 0, "ZERO_ASSETS") in withdraw and require(receiver != address(0)) in both entry points. Emit and return consistently.

findings.title: Not actually ERC-4626: withdraw() is a redeem-by-shares, and the preview/max/mint/redeem surface is absent
findings.where: deposit() L57, withdraw() L66, constructor L23-L35
findings.detail: The block is described as ERC4626-shaped, but withdraw(uint256 shares, address receiver) takes shares (4626 withdraw takes assets and redeem takes shares), there is no mint/redeem/previewDeposit/previewWithdraw/maxDeposit/maxWithdraw and no asset()-style accessor beyond the public immutable. Any external 4626 integrator (routers, aggregators, other vaults) will call the wrong semantics or fail. The share token also copies the asset's decimals via IERC20(asset_).decimals(), so deployment reverts for assets without decimals() and share balances inherit low-precision units (6 decimals for USDC), which worsens rounding in the conversions.
findings.exploit: Not exploitable on its own; a 4626 router calling withdraw(assetsAmount, receiver) burns assetsAmount SHARES instead, over- or under-withdrawing the user by the share price ratio.
findings.recommendation: Either implement the full ERC-4626 interface (asset(), mint, redeem, preview*, max*, withdraw-by-assets) or stop labelling the block 4626 and name the function redeem(). Consider a decimalsOffset so shares carry more precision than the asset.

findings.title: Composition: the share token's price is manipulable in-block, so do not wire it as collateral or as an oracle source downstream
findings.where: totalAssets() L38-L42 (price source for the erc20 output)
findings.detail: The vault's erc20 output can be wired into staking, an AMM pair, lending or CDP blocks. Its redemption value is a live function of balanceOf(vault) and strategy.totalAssets(), both of which can be moved within one transaction by a donation (VAULT-1), by the owner (VAULT-2, VAULT-5) or by unbacked accrual (VAULT-3). A lending/CDP block that values vault shares by convertToAssets() or by an AMM spot price can be made to accept inflated collateral or to liquidate healthy positions.
findings.exploit: 1) Attacker holds vault shares and posts them as collateral in a downstream lending block that prices them via convertToAssets(). 2) Attacker donates assets to the vault (or the owner points to a strategy that over-reports) to inflate convertToAssets() in the same block. 3) Attacker borrows against the inflated value, then withdraws the donation-derived value through the vault, leaving the lender under-collateralised.
findings.recommendation: Treat mv* shares as an unpriced token in the composer: only wire them into blocks that do not derive value from them (staking rewards, plain transfers). If a price is needed, use a TWAP/oracle block with staleness bounds rather than convertToAssets() or an AMM spot read.

safe_use: Seed the vault yourself immediately after deployment (deposit a meaningful amount, e.g. 1_000 units, and never withdraw that position) so no attacker can be the first depositor; verify convertToShares(1e18) is sane before announcing it.
Wire the governor port to the timelock block (or a multisig) so setStrategy, allocate and setOwner are visible before they execute; an EOA owner is fully custodial over every deposit.

Only attach the catalog ModFixedYieldStrategy after calling fund() with at least rateBps * principal / 10_000 for the intended horizon, and keep the reserve ahead of accrual; run a deposit or withdraw periodically so unbacked _pending() cannot drift.
Do not rely on performanceFeeBps: harvest() collects nothing in this version. Set it to 0 to avoid misleading the UI, or patch harvest with a high-water mark first.

Never call setStrategy while funds are allocated; there is no deallocate. Drain via withdrawals (or a full-exit from the strategy side) before rotating, and never leave the vault with totalSupply > 0 and totalAssets() == 0.
Use only plain ERC20 assets that return bool (the catalog token block is fine); fee-on-transfer, rebasing and USDT-style tokens are unsupported.
Do not use the share token as collateral in lending/CDP blocks or as an AMM-priced oracle source; its price is movable within one transaction.
